parole.testo: Borrowed from German Agronom, from Ancient Greek ἀγρονόμος (agronómos), from ἀγρός (agrós, “field”). With Latinate -us ending.

parole.significato: acrostic (poem or other text in which certain letters, often the first in each line, spell out a name or message)
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Akrostichon (“acrostic”), from Ancient Greek ἀκρόστιχον (akróstikhon).

parole.significato: acoustics (the science of sounds, teaching their nature, phenomena and laws)
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Akustik. Ultimately from Ancient Greek ἀκουστικός (akoustikós).

parole.significato: aliphatic (of a class of organic compounds in which the carbon atoms are arranged in an open chain)
parole.testo: Borrowed from German aliphatisch (“aliphatic”) + -s (adjective-forming suffix), ultimately from Ancient Greek ἄλειφᾰρ (áleiphăr, “oil, ointment”).
Borrowed from German Allergie, coinage crafted using Ancient Greek ἄλλος (állos, “other”) + ἔργον (érgon, “work, activity”).
From German Analphabet (“illiterate”), coined from Ancient Greek ἀν- (an-, “not”) + ἀλφάβητος (alphábētos, “alphabet”).
From German Anion, from Ancient Greek ἀνιόν (anión, “(thing) going up”), neuter past participle of ἄνειμι (áneimi, “go up”), from ἀνά (aná, “up”) + εἶμι (eîmi, “go”).
Borrowed from German Apatit, from Ancient Greek ἀπάτη (apátē, “deceit, deception”).
From German aromatisch, from Ancient Greek ἀρωματικός (arōmatikós, “aromatic”).

parole.significato: atmosphere (the gases surrounding the Earth or any astronomical body)
parole.testo: From German Atmosphäre, from Ancient Greek ἀτμός (atmós, “steam”) + σφαῖρα (sphaîra, “sphere”).

From German Automat, from Ancient Greek αὐτόματον (autómaton), neuter of αὐτόματος (autómatos, “self-moving, moving of oneself, self-acting, spontaneous”), from αὐτός (autós, “self, myself”) + μέμαα (mémaa, “to wish eagerly, strive, yearn, desire”).
Borrowed from German demokratisch, from Ancient Greek δημοκρατικός (dēmokratikós, “of or for democracy", "favoring or suited for democracy”). With Latinate -ikus ending.

parole.significato: diapositive, slide (transparent plate used with a projector for projecting images)
parole.testo: From German Diapositiv, from Ancient Greek δια- (dia-, “across, through”).

parole.significato: didactics (the theory of education and instruction)
parole.testo: From German Didaktik, from Ancient Greek διδακτικη (τέχνη) (didaktikē (tékhnē), “teaching (art)”).
Borrowed from German dynamisch, from Ancient Greek δυναμικός (dunamikós, “powerful”), from δύναμις (dúnamis, “power”). With Latinate -ikus ending.

parole.significato: dramaturge (a person in a coordinative function at theatre or film productions)
parole.testo: From German Dramaturg, from Ancient Greek δραματουργός (dramatourgós, “dramatist, playwright”).

Borrowed from German eklektisch, from Ancient Greek ἐκλεκτικός (eklektikós, “selective”), from ἐκλέγω (eklégō, “I pick, choose”), from ἐκ (ek, “out, from”) + λέγω (légō, “I choose, count”). With Latinate -ikus ending.
Borrowed from German erotisch, from Ancient Greek ἐρωτικός (erōtikós, “related to love”). With Latinate -ikus ending.

parole.significato: Ethiopian (of, from, or relating to Ethiopia, the Ethiopian people or the Ethiopian culture)
parole.testo: From German Äthiopien, from Ancient Greek Αἰθίοψ (Aithíops, “charred complexion”), from αἴθω (aíthō, “I burn”) + ὤψ (ṓps, “eye, face, complexion”).
Borrowed from German gigantisch, from Ancient Greek γιγαντικός (gigantikós). With Latinate -ikus ending.
From German Graphem (“grapheme”), ultimately from Ancient Greek γράφω (gráphō, “to write”).

parole.significato: heterogeneous (diverse in kind or nature; composed of diverse parts)
parole.testo: From German heterogen, from Ancient Greek ἑτερογενής (heterogenḗs, “of different kinds”), from ἕτερος (héteros, “other, another, different”) + γένος (génos, “kind”).
From German Kaleidoskop, from Ancient Greek καλός (kalós, “beautiful”) + εἶδος (eîdos, “shape”).
Borrowed from German Kalligraphie, from Ancient Greek καλλιγραφία (kalligraphía, literally “pretty writing”), from κάλλος (kállos, “beauty”) + γράφω (gráphō, “write, draw”). With -gráfia ending.
From German Kation, from Ancient Greek κατά (katá, “down”) + ἰόν (ión, “going”).
From German Kathode, from Ancient Greek κατα- (kata-, “down”) and ὁδός (hodós, “journey, way”), forming the New Greek compound κάθοδος (káthodos, “way down, descent”).

parole.significato: kinematics (the branch of mechanics concerned with objects in motion, but not with the forces involved)
parole.testo: From German Kinematik, from Ancient Greek κίνημα (kínēma, “motion”).
From German Choreographie, from Ancient Greek χορεία (khoreía, “dance”) + -γραφία (-graphía, “written form (of a word, etc.), spelling”). With -gráfia ending.

From German Kosmetiker (“cosmetician”) and kosmetisch (“cosmetic”), from Ancient Greek κοσμητικός (kosmētikós, “relating to adornment”), from κοσμέω (kosméō, “I arrange, adorn”). With Latinate -ikus ending.

parole.significato: lexeme (unit of vocabulary, the different forms of the same lemma)
parole.testo: From German Lexem, from Ancient Greek λέξις (léxis, “word”).
From German metaphorisch, ultimately from Ancient Greek μεταφορά (metaphorá). With -ikus ending.
Borrowed from German mythisch, from Ancient Greek μῡθῐκός (mūthĭkós). With Latinate -ikus ending.
From German Oktaeder, from Ancient Greek ὀκτώ (oktṓ, “eight”) + ἕδρα (hédra, “seat”).
From German orthodox, from Ancient Greek ὀρθόδοξος (orthódoxos), from ὀρθός (orthós, “straight”) + δόξα (dóxa, “opinion”).
From German paradox, from Ancient Greek παράδοξος (parádoxos, “unexpected, strange”).
Borrowed from German polemisch, from Ancient Greek πολεμικός (polemikós, “of war”). With Latinate -ikus ending.

parole.significato: polygon (a plane figure bounded by edges that are all straight lines)
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Polygon. Ultimately from Ancient Greek πολύγωνον (polúgōnon), from πολύς (polús, “many”) and γωνία (gōnía, “angle”).

parole.significato: stadium (venue where sporting events are held)
parole.testo: From German Stadion (“stadium”), from Ancient Greek στάδιον (stádion).
From German Skepsis, from Ancient Greek σκέψις (sképsis, “examination, observation, consideration”), from σκέπτομαι (sképtomai, “I consider”).
Borrowed from German skeptisch, from Ancient Greek σκεπτικός (skeptikós, “thoughtful, inquiring”). With Latinate -ikus ending.
Borrowed from German Stereotypie. Ultimately from Ancient Greek στερεός (stereós, “solid”) + τῠ́πος (tŭ́pos, “mark, impression, type”).
From German Stöchiometrie, from Ancient Greek στοιχεῖον (stoikheîon, “element”).

parole.significato: tetrahedron (a polyhedron composed of four triangular faces, six straight edges, and four vertex corners)
parole.testo: From German Tetraeder, from Ancient Greek τετράεδρον (tetráedron, “triangle-based pyramid”), from τετράεδρος (tetráedros), from τετράς (tetrás, “four”) + ἕδρα (hédra, “seat”).
vér (“blood”) + tanú (“witness”), calque of German Blutzeuge, itself influenced by Ancient Greek μάρτυς (mártus, “witness, martyr”)
Internationalism via German Ozon (“ozone”), from Ancient Greek ὄζον (ózon), neuter participle of ὄζω (ózō, “to smell”). First attested in 1846.
From German Ökologie, from Ancient Greek οἶκος (oîkos, “house”) + -λογία (-logía, “study of”). With -lógia ending.
